title: Religious Law and State Law
objective: After this level you can compare how Jewish law, church law and sharia work, and how religious law has shaped or sits beside the laws of modern states.
summary: Halakhah, canon law and sharia are three great systems of religious law. Each is worked out by scholars, binds believers, and sits beside the laws of modern states rather than replacing them.

cards.headline: Who writes the law when believers say the lawgiver is God?
cards.body: Many faiths guide daily life with law, not only belief. Meet three great systems of religious law, see how scholars work each one out, and find where each meets the laws of a modern state.

cards.headline: Halakhah: the Way
cards.body: Jewish law is called halakhah, Hebrew for "the Way". It reaches well beyond courtrooms, into religious observance and daily conduct, such as keeping the Sabbath. Jews trace it to the revelation at Sinai; it grew through the Mishnah, compiled in the early 3rd century CE, and then the Talmud. Today Jews read it differently: Orthodox and Conservative Judaism treat it as binding, with Conservative rabbis adapting some laws, while Reform Judaism holds most of it not binding.

cards.headline: Canon law: a church's own rulebook
cards.body: Canon law is law made by church authority to govern a church and its members. The Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches all have it. Notice whom it binds: canon 11 of the Catholic Code of Canon Law says purely church laws bind those baptized in or received into the Catholic Church. The state isn't bound at all, though canon law left its mark on secular law, from marriage law to criminal procedure.

cards.headline: Sharia is the path; fiqh is the map-making
cards.body: For Muslims, sharia is a divinely ordained path of conduct, covering their relationship with God, like prayer and fasting, as well as dealings with neighbors and the state. Scholars derive it from the Quran and the Sunnah, the Prophet's example, adding consensus and analogy. That human work is called fiqh, "understanding". Because it is human work, the schools of law hold a wide range of positions on almost every point.

cards.headline: Religious law beside the state
cards.body: So where does religious law meet a modern government? From the 19th century, most Muslim countries adopted Western-style criminal codes and kept sharia mainly for family law: marriage, divorce and inheritance. Put that next to canon law, which binds church members but not the state, and a pattern appears: the believer's law and the state's law run side by side.

cards.headline: Religious Law and State Law: the takeaways
learned: Halakhah, 'the Way', is Jewish law for observance and daily life
Canon law binds a church's members, not the state
Sharia is the path; fiqh is the human work of understanding it

questions.prompt: What does halakhah, the Hebrew name for Jewish law, mean?

options.label: The Book
options.rationale: Halakhah names a way of living, not a book.

options.label: The Court
options.rationale: It reaches far beyond courts, into daily life.

questions.explanation: Halakhah means "the Way": law for religious observance and daily conduct.

questions.prompt: A newly independent country follows the pattern most Muslim countries adopted from the 1800s. Where would sharia most likely apply?

options.label: In every criminal trial
options.rationale: Most adopted Western-style criminal codes instead.

options.label: In family matters such as marriage, divorce and inheritance
Only in banking and trade
options.rationale: The pattern kept sharia mainly for family law.

options.label: Nowhere in state law at all
options.rationale: Most kept it for family law.

questions.explanation: Most Muslim countries adopted Western-style criminal codes and kept sharia mainly for family law.

questions.prompt: Halakhah, canon law and sharia belong most clearly to which of Smart's seven dimensions from Level 3?

options.label: Material
options.rationale: That covers buildings, art and sacred places.

options.label: Experience and emotion
options.rationale: These are rules for conduct, not feelings.

questions.explanation: Smart's ethical and legal dimension covers the rules a tradition lives by, and all three are bodies of religious law.
